newsitem.title: USA: EPA to seek extra $1.3 bln for Superfund 1998, '99.
newsitem.headline: EPA to seek extra $1.3 bln for Superfund 1998, '99.

text.p: The Clinton administration is set to ask Congress for an extra $1.3 billion for the Superfund toxic waste cleanup program spread over the 1998 and 1999 fiscal years, according to EPA officials.
Congress last year approved a budget of $1.3 billion for Superfund cleanup projects for the 1997 fiscal year, about the same amount as in the previous few years.
During his re-election campaign, President Clinton said he wanted to expand funding for the program to speed up cleanups.
The request for more funding is bound to touch off debate to renew Superfund taxes that expired in 1995, lobbyists said.
An EPA spokeswoman said the 1998 budget request, to be released in two weeks, assumed that the defunct Superfund oil, chemical and corporate taxes would be renewed.

Those taxes of about $1.4 billion a year used to make up 70 percent of the money going into the Superfund trust fund, tapped to run and pay for cleanups where polluters could not be found or could not pay.

Republican leaders refused to renew the taxes until Congress overhauled the Superfund cleanup law. Efforts last year ground to a halt as Democrats refused to back proposals that would have shifted most cleanup costs to the government.

The Congressional Budget Office last year estimated there was enough money in the trust fund to last until 2000 without renewing the taxes if Superfund spending was held at around $1.3 billion a year.
Industry officials said Tuesday that by seeking more funding in 1998 and 1999, the agency was forcing Congress's hand to renew the taxes.
"It puts the heat directly back on the Republicans. If they run out of money, they have to turn the tax on again," said one oil industry lobbyist.
If the Republicans let the trust fund run dry and let the Superfund program die, they would be accused of putting the environment at risk, he said.
